decisions.quote: A previous study with Virtual Reality (VR) and online motion-capture quantified this approach bias towards food and non-food cues in a controlled VR environment with hand movements. The aim of this study was to test the specificity of a manual approach bias for high-calorie food in grasp movements compared to low-calorie food and neutral objects of different complexity, namely, simple balls and geometrically more complex office tools.

decisions.quote: A previous study with Virtual Reality (VR) and online motion-capture quantified this approach bias towards food and non-food cues in a controlled VR environment with hand movements. The aim of this study was to test the specificity of a manual approach bias for high-calorie food in grasp movements compared to low-calorie food and neutral objects of different complexity, namely, simple balls and geometrically more complex office tools.
decisions.reason: The 2024 source supplies only the abstract (N = 27 healthy participants performing VR grasp/collection and push/warding movements with high-calorie food, low-calorie food, balls, and office tools) and deposited reference list (bib1-bib73), without the full text or in-text citations. Complete primary texts were inspected for the two candidate VR hand-movement food-bias studies in the bibliography: (1) bib60, Schroeder, Lohmann, Butz, & Plewnia (2016, 10.1089/cyber.2015.0311, shipped row 1827; complete accepted manuscript in 19_lohmann_thesis.unrepaired.txt Appendix A), which tested 23 recruited/20 analyzed healthy participants in a VR + Leap Motion grasp/ward task with high-calorie food and balls, finding faster movement onset (p = .05), contact (p = .05), and grasp collection for food than balls (t(19) = 3.692, p = .002) while noting object complexity as an open limitation; and (2) bib39, Max, Schroeder, Blechert, Giel, Ehlis, & Plewnia (2021, 10.1007/s00429-021-02232-9; 02_max_fulltext.all_text.unrepaired.txt), an explicit follow-up (33 recruited/30 analyzed) using VR + Leap Motion (with fNIRS) and touchscreen category selection with food, balls, and office tools, finding faster food movement onset (p = .043) and touch (p = .017) but slower VR food collection (p < .001) in explicit contrast to Schroeder et al. (2016). Although the 2024 grasp/ward task and faster collection finding align more closely with Schroeder et al. (2016), task differences alone do not exclude Max et al. (2021) from the retested chain, and without the 2024 body's in-text citations, unique attribution to row 1827 cannot be conclusively established.
